title: Longest Turbulent Subarray
description: Brute force to optimized: validating every candidate window's alternation directly versus dual Kadane's-style streaks, one per direction.

blocks.text: Given an integer array arr, return the length of the longest TURBULENT subarray: a contiguous subarray where the comparison between every pair of adjacent elements strictly alternates between "greater than" and "less than" (never staying the same direction twice in a row, and never equal).

blocks.caption: Track two running streaks in parallel: one ending on an "up" step, one ending on a "down" step

blocks.text: Given an integer array arr, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray where every adjacent pair of elements alternates between strictly increasing and strictly decreasing.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Longest Unbroken Zigzag Walk
blocks.text: Like walking along a path with varying elevation and tracking the longest unbroken zigzag: up, then down, then up, then down, with no two consecutive steps going the same direction and no flat steps allowed at all. Since each step can only continue a zigzag if it goes the OPPOSITE direction of the step before it, tracking "longest zigzag ending here, going up" and "longest zigzag ending here, going down" separately captures both possibilities cleanly.

blocks.caption: An up-step can only extend a streak that just went down, and vice versa; equal steps reset both

blocks.text: Edge case: arr has only one element
A single element has no adjacent pairs to compare at all, so it is trivially turbulent (vacuously), giving an answer of 1.
Before checking every possible subarray's alternation directly, notice that whether a new step extends a turbulent streak depends entirely on whether the PREVIOUS step went the opposite direction.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A new "up" step (arr[i] > arr[i-1]) can only ever extend a turbulent streak whose last step was "down" (since two ups in a row breaks alternation); similarly, a new "down" step can only extend a streak whose last step was "up".

Observation 2: This means two parallel running values are needed: up (length of the turbulent streak ending here, with its last step being an increase) and down (length ending here, with its last step being a decrease).

Observation 3: At each new comparison, exactly one of the two streaks gets extended (using the OTHER streak's previous value, plus 1), while the other resets to 1, since it can no longer be validly continued.

Observation 4: If two adjacent elements are equal, alternation is broken entirely, and BOTH streaks reset to 1.

Recognizing this as Kadane's "extend or reset" recurrence, doubled to track both possible directions in parallel, is what collapses an apparently expensive multi-directional check into a single linear pass.
This is Kadane's Algorithm generalized to track two mutually-exclusive running streaks simultaneously, since the direction of the very next needed step alternates with every extension.
For every possible pair of starting and ending indices, check directly whether every adjacent comparison within that range alternates correctly.

items: For every possible (start, end) pair, walk through every adjacent comparison within that range.
A candidate window is valid only if no two adjacent elements are equal, and no two consecutive comparisons go the same direction.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every (start, end) pair is tried explicitly, since this brute force does not yet share work between overlapping candidate windows.
Both the equality check and the direction-alternation check are performed for every adjacent pair within a candidate window, since either violation invalidates the whole window.
best is updated only for windows that pass both checks entirely.

blocks.text: Every possible subarray is checked directly for full alternation, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed) in the worst case, since there are O(n squared) candidate windows, each requiring up to O(n) work to validate.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: re-validating every adjacent comparison from scratch for every candidate window ignores that whether a given comparison extends a turbulent streak depends only on the single comparison right before it, exactly like Kadane's Algorithm.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force re-validates every candidate window from scratch. Instead, maintain two running streak lengths simultaneously: up (ending on an increasing step) and down (ending on a decreasing step). At each new comparison, exactly one of these extends from the OTHER's previous value (since alternation requires switching direction), while the other resets to 1. On an equal comparison, both reset to 1. Track the maximum of both streaks throughout a single linear pass.

Maintain up and down, both initialized to 1. At each position i (from the second element onward), if arr[i] > arr[i-1], set up = down + 1 and down = 1; if arr[i] < arr[i-1], set down = up + 1 and up = 1; if equal, reset both to 1. Track best as the maximum of up and down seen throughout.
Track two running streaks in parallel, swapping which one extends based on the direction of each new comparison.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with O(1) work per element.
Space: O(1) extra.

An increasing step can only validly continue a turbulent streak whose most recent step was decreasing (never one that was also increasing), so up is correctly computed from down's PREVIOUS value plus 1; the symmetric argument holds for down being computed from up's previous value. Since the two streaks are mutually exclusive by construction (a streak's last step is either up or down, never both), tracking them in parallel and taking their maximum at every position covers every possible turbulent subarray.

items: up and down are both initialized to 1, since a single element is trivially a turbulent subarray of length 1.
Exactly one of up/down is ever extended per iteration; the other is always reset, since a streak's direction cannot repeat twice in a row by definition.
best is updated every iteration by comparing against both up and down, since the true longest turbulent subarray could end with either direction.

blocks.text: This problem generalizes Kadane's "extend or reset" recurrence to two mutually-exclusive parallel streaks, since alternation means each new step's validity depends on the OPPOSITE-direction streak's previous length, not its own.

items: Tracking only a single running streak, missing that an "up" step and a "down" step require entirely separate state to track correctly.
Extending up from up's own previous value (or down from down's own) instead of swapping, which would incorrectly allow two same-direction steps in a row.
Forgetting the equal-elements case, which must reset BOTH streaks to 1, not just skip the comparison.

items: Explicitly explain why up must be computed from down's PREVIOUS value (and vice versa), since this cross-referencing is the one subtle detail that most easily gets mixed up when first deriving the recurrence.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Longest run where a comparison must strictly ALTERNATE direction" points toward tracking two parallel Kadane's-style streaks, one per direction, each extending from the OTHER's previous value.

items: How would you also report the actual turbulent subarray, not just its length? Track a tentative start index for each streak, resetting it whenever that streak resets, and record the (start, end) pair whenever best is updated.

How would this generalize to requiring a specific PERIOD of alternation (e.g., up-up-down-up-up-down repeating)? A more general state machine tracking "position within the required pattern" would replace the simple two-streak approach.

What if equal adjacent elements were allowed to count as "either direction"? The reset-to-1 behavior on equality would need to change to something more permissive, likely requiring careful case analysis to avoid double-counting.

A dual-streak generalization of Kadane's Algorithm / Longest Continuous Increasing Subsequence, tracking two mutually-exclusive running values instead of one, in the same broad "extend or reset" family.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n cubed) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (dual Kadane's-style streaks): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Dual Kadane's-style streak tracking: one running value for streaks ending on an "up" step, one for "down"
Core Idea: An up-step can only extend a streak that just went down, and vice versa; equal elements reset both streaks
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Because direction must strictly alternate, each streak can only ever be extended using the OTHER direction's previous length
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: up = down + 1 on an increase, down = up + 1 on a decrease, both reset to 1 on equal
